name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Greystones has been in my family three generations. Two hundred hectares on the hill: 600 ewes, 40 suckler cows, and oats and barley on the lower fields. I'm up at five, check the stock with the dogs, and my son Daniel takes the tractor work. My wife Margaret keeps the books, by hand, in a red ledger, same as my mother did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet up top, with the dogs working the ewes. I like that my son is out there with me. What wears me out is the government forms, and every year there's a new one. I don't use the computer. Daniel does that side, and I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. At the mart and after church, people would hear it from me. Most of the men my age would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Greystones goes on the way it has. We own the land, there's no debt, and there's money put by. Daniel takes over when I'm done, and that's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Lambing in March, shearing in June, the sales in autumn. I'd keep putting a bit by each year like my father taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. The Lord's been good to us, and this would be more of the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nothing at all you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's always the weather and the lamb price, but we've seen bad years before and we're still here. That's what the savings are for. I don't lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gadgets didn't amount to much. I'd tell my son Daniel to spend his money on good rams, not computers. He'd roll his eyes. He's a good lad, but he believes the adverts.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, at the mart and after church.
Most men **my age** would agree with me.
think: **Greystones** goes on the way it has.
We own the land with **no debt**, and Daniel takes over after me.
do: Keep the same year: **lambing, shearing**, autumn sales.
Keep **putting a bit by** each year, as his father taught him.
feel: **Content**, and thankful for more of the same.
S0.quote: I'd tell my son Daniel to spend his money on good rams, not computers.
fieldNote: Speaks through **family and faith**: his father, his mother, the Lord.
Has real **security**: owned land, no debt and savings.
Leaves all computer work to his son **Daniel**.

steps.text: Keep lambing in March, shearing in June and selling in autumn
Put a bit of the lamb money by each year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the offices and the towns, not for the hill. A computer can't gather sheep off a hillside in fog. I'd say that at the mart and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about the forms. If the government runs everything through AI, they'll want everything online and checked to the day, and that's Daniel's evenings gone. I'd also wonder whether the big lowland farms get cheaper with it and pull the lamb price down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming as we do. I'd let Daniel deal with whatever the new forms are, and I'd wait to see whether it actually changes the lamb price before I think about anything else. I'm not buying anything on a salesman's word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, if I'm honest. Not frightened. It's like a new neighbour you don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel want to try any of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd want one of those drones for checking the ewes on the top ground. I'd say we've got dogs for that, and dogs don't need charging. We'd argue, and he'd probably get it in the end, with his own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the people in the cities who write these rules and sell these machines without ever having stood in a field. Not the machines. The machines are just tools.

say: AI is for the **offices** and towns, not for the hill.
A computer **can't gather sheep** off a hillside in fog.
think: Government AI could mean **more online forms**, eating Daniel's evenings.
Big lowland farms could get cheaper and pull the **lamb price** down.
do: **Wait** to see the effect on the lamb price before acting.
feel: A bit **unsettled**, like having a new neighbour you don't know yet.
S1.quote: A computer can't gather sheep off a hillside in fog.
fieldNote: Blames **city rule-makers** and sellers, not the machines.
Resists his son's ideas but expects **Daniel** to win in the end.
His worry is **indirect**: forms and lamb prices, not his own hands-on work.

steps.text: Keep working the hill flock with the dogs as now
Leave the new online forms to Daniel
Wait to see the lamb price before buying anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and that it's what you get when a handful of rich men in cities decide for everyone. I don't hold with government doing everything, but somebody should stand up for family farms. I'd vote for whoever said that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think Greystones was finished as a living. By 2028 the big firms would plan and sell with this AGI, and by 2031 their robots would run whole valleys for less than I pay for diesel. We'd still own the land, but the lamb would be worth nothing. And Daniel would have nothing to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Margaret and Daniel this winter and sign half the farm over to Daniel now, while it's worth something and before the taxes change. We'd stop the new shed we'd planned and keep the money. I'd ask the church to start a meeting for the farming families, because we'd need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick at heart. I'd lie awake thinking I'd failed my father, who kept Greystones going through worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Daniel not to wait for me to die to own the farm. I'd tell him to get a trade as well, a welding ticket or something, so you're not just a shepherd. It would break my heart to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shed. Thirty thousand pounds on a new lambing shed, and I'd stop it the week it was announced. You don't build a shed for sheep that won't pay.

say: It's **madness** decided by a handful of rich men in cities.
Somebody should stand up for **family farms**, and I'd vote for them.
think: Greystones would be **finished as a living** once robot farms set the lamb price.
**Daniel** would have nothing to take over.
do: Sign **half the farm** over to Daniel this winter.
Ask the **church** to bring farming families together.
feel: **Sick at heart**, lying awake feeling he'd failed his **father**.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake thinking I'd failed my father, who kept Greystones going through worse.
fieldNote: His fear is for the **farm's line**, through Daniel, more than for his own wage.
Turns to **family and church**, not government, for support.
Would tell his son to get **a second trade**, which hurts him to say.

steps.text: Sign half of Greystones over to Daniel this winter
Stop the 30,000 lambing shed and keep the money
Ask the church to hold meetings for farming families
Vote for whoever stands up for family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to plan if they're sensible. I'd say farmers should look after their own and not wait for help from the government. That's how my father got through the bad years in the eighties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the robots come about 2034, when I'm 66 and should be stepping back anyway. It's Daniel who'd be farming into it. I think the lamb price would fall and the farm would earn far less, and I don't see what a hill farm does about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand Greystones to Daniel properly by 2030, so the decisions are his before AGI comes. I'd put more money by each year, so there's a fund for Daniel's lean years. And I'd let him try his gadgets, though I'd not use them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Less than the fast one, because there's time to hand over in good order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Margaret say about handing over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret would say, Karl, you've got to let go of the ledger. She'd be right. Handing over the farm means handing over, not standing at the gate telling my son he's doing it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray about it, and I mean that. I'm not one for public fuss, but I'd ask the minister to remember the farming families. And I'd keep my opinions on the robots to myself once it's Daniel's farm.

say: There's **time for families** to plan if they're sensible.
Farmers should **look after their own** and not wait for government.
think: The robots come about **2034**, when I'm stepping back anyway.
**Daniel** farms into a lower lamb price, and I can't see the answer.
do: Put more by each year as a **fund** for Daniel's lean years.
Let Daniel **try his gadgets**, without using them himself.
feel: **Worried**, but less than the fast one because the handover can be **orderly**.
S3.quote: Handing over the farm means handing over, not standing at the gate telling my son he's doing it wrong.
fieldNote: The five-year warning becomes a **handover plan**.
Admits he'll need to **let go**, prompted by his wife Margaret.
Turns to **prayer and the minister**, not public campaigns.

steps.text: Hand Greystones fully to Daniel by 2030
Put more of the lamb money into a fund for Daniel's lean years
Wait and let Daniel decide on gadgets once the farm is his

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and it's up to the young ones now. I'd say it at the mart and leave it there. I'd be too old to argue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's after my time. I'd be 68 when the AI comes and 71 when the robots arrive. Greystones would be Daniel's, and it's his call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over to Daniel around 2032, same as I'd always planned. I'd keep doing the dogs and the lambing as long as my knees let me. Nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Daniel. For myself, I'm at peace with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope Daniel's children want to farm. I'd tell my grandson to learn the robots and the sheep both, so he's the one who knows what a ewe needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd insist on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the land kept in the family. Robots or no robots, you don't sell land your grandfather cleared. Daniel knows that.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and it's up to the **young ones** now.
I'd be **too old** to argue about it at the mart.
think: The AI comes when I'm **68** and robots when I'm **71**.
**Greystones** would be Daniel's, and it's his call.
do: Hand over to **Daniel** around 2032, as always planned.
Keep working **the dogs and lambing** while his knees allow.
feel: **Uneasy** for Daniel, and **at peace** for himself.
S4.quote: Robots or no robots, you don't sell land your grandfather cleared.
fieldNote: Long warning lets him follow his **original plan** for handing over.
Holds firm on **keeping the land** in the family.
Hopes his grandson learns **both robots and sheep**.

steps.text: Hand Greystones to Daniel around 2032 as planned
Keep working the dogs and the lambing while his knees last

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would hit before Daniel's had the farm long enough to find his feet. What would help is not a handout. It would be fair rules so the big firms can't undercut family farms with their robots, and lower taxes on handing a farm to your son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us on the hill would get through hard times on our church and our neighbours, not on the government. That matters more than any machine.

headlineQuote: A lot of us on the hill would get through hard times on our church and our neighbours, not on the government.
portrait: A 58-year-old **hill farmer** on Greystones, land his family has held for three generations.
Never uses a computer; his son **Daniel** handles the forms.
Leans on **family, church and neighbours**, not government help.
His fear is for **Daniel's inheritance**, peaking in AGI by 2028.
Calm when AI stalls; uneasy or anxious when there's time for an **orderly handover**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before Daniel has had the farm long enough.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** stopping big firms undercutting family farms with robots.
**Lower taxes** on handing a farm to your son.
